title: Muslim League Attack on Sikhs and Hindus in the Punjab, 1947
byline: compiled by S. Gurbachan Singh Talib, Principal of Lyallpur Khalsa College · Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, 1950 · Voice of India reprint, 1991, with an introduction by Ram Swarup
lede: Compiled in 1947 and published in 1950 by the SGPC, the body that manages Sikh gurdwaras, this is a record of the uprooting of more than seven million Hindus and Sikhs from West Punjab, the Frontier, Sindh and the parts of Kashmir held by raiders. Talib argues that the violence was planned by the Muslim League to make Pakistan purely Muslim, and he answers the League's claim that Sikhs started it. Half the book is evidence: about fifty eyewitness statements and official reports, and a numbered list of almost 600 atrocities.

note: This is a partisan record from one side of the Partition massacres, compiled to assign blame. Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims all committed and suffered atrocities in 1947, including in East Punjab. Historians estimate that between several hundred thousand and two million people died across the subcontinent. This page summarises what this book documents and argues, without its graphic detail.

sections.title: From Direct Action to the Kashmir raid
items: Talib traces the League's aim of a Muslim state “not encumbered” with non-Muslims.
Called by the League after the Cabinet Mission plan, followed by the Calcutta killings.
Villages attacked, including Thoha Khalsa. The gurdwara at Dehra Sahib attacked.
Talib argues the League ignored it in practice.
Amritsar and then “West Punjab ablaze”: Sheikhupura, Gujranwala, Lyallpur, Sharaqpur.
Attacks on trains, abductions, forced conversions.
Reports by the Chief Liaison Officer.
Found razed after the raiders retreated (Hindustan Times).

sections.title: Places named in the eyewitness accounts
Two questions Talib answers
items: Did Sikhs and Hindus leave Pakistan voluntarily?
No. He argues they were driven out by planned violence.
He rejects the League's charge that Sikhs prepared the massacres, and presents Sikh violence as retaliation.

sections.title: What kinds of documents the book collects
items: Widows, girls, policemen and tehsildars, mostly recorded by the Chief Liaison Officers in Lahore.
